entries.meaning: The modal of future time, willingness and prediction — and the one that contracts to 'll so reliably that learners stop hearing it.
examples: The package will arrive on Thursday.
She said the meeting would run long, and it did.
I will be at the airport by six.
I 'll carry that for you.
The car won't start in this cold.
He promised he would call the moment he landed.
Will you hold the elevator?
Would you mind closing the window?
Will you please stop doing that.
He will sit there for hours without saying a word.
Accidents will happen.
She would always bring something from her garden.

senses.head: Future time
body: The neutral way to put an event after now. With 'll in speech almost always. (буду, будет)
examples: The package will arrive on Thursday.
She said the meeting would run long, and it did.
I will be at the airport by six.

senses.head: Willingness, offers and promises
body: Not time at all — consent. The negative won't is a refusal, and it is used of objects too. (соглашаться; обещать)
examples: I 'll carry that for you.
The car won't start in this cold.
He promised he would call the moment he landed.

senses.head: Requests — Will you…?
body: A direct request. Would you is the softer version, which is why it is far commoner. (не могли бы вы)
examples: Will you hold the elevator?
Would you mind closing the window?
Will you please stop doing that.

senses.head: Characteristic behavior
body: A habit presented as typical rather than scheduled — often mildly critical when stressed. (бывает, имеет обыкновение)
examples: He will sit there for hours without saying a word.
Accidents will happen.
She would always bring something from her garden.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /wəl/, contracted 'll /l/ in I'll go
entries.русский: вспомогательный глагол будущего времени; выражает согласие, обещание
entries.register: everyday — the most common modal in the language
entries.pattern: i — ou (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: will — no -s, ✗ he wills · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: English has no future tense — it has will plus a bare infinitive, which is why will is a modal and not an ending. Russian speakers reach for it too often: after when, if, as soon as, until and before, English uses the present, ✗ when I will arrive → when I arrive. A separate and fully regular verb will means "leave by will" (she willed the house to her niece), and the noun will means both "testament" and "willpower".
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — takes a bare infinitive (will go), has no -s, no -ing, no participle (✗ he wills go, ✗ I have would, ✗ to will). Be going to and the present progressive fill in where a stance about the future is not wanted.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — a modal takes a bare-infinitive complement, not an object. Bare will with a noun (I will it to happen) is the separate regular verb.
entries.passive: no — the verb it supports carries the voice: the letter will be sent, never will itself.

entries.meaning: The workhorse of conditionals, polite requests and remembered habit — and the reason I would like sounds courteous where I want sounds blunt.
examples: If I had the money, I would buy it outright.
She would have told you if she had known.
What would you do in my place?
Would you pass me the salt?
I would like a table by the window, please.
Would you rather wait outside?
Every summer we would drive up to the lake.
My grandfather would read the paper cover to cover.
She would never admit she was tired.
He said he would be late.
They promised the parts would ship on Monday.
I knew she would say that.

senses.head: The hypothetical result
body: The main clause of a conditional: if + past, then would + bare infinitive. (бы)
examples: If I had the money, I would buy it outright.
She would have told you if she had known.
What would you do in my place?

senses.head: Polite requests and offers
body: Present time, not past. Would you and I would like are the two politest frames in everyday English. (не могли бы; хотел бы)
examples: Would you pass me the salt?
I would like a table by the window, please.
Would you rather wait outside?

senses.head: Past habit
body: A repeated action in a finished stretch of the past. Unlike used to, would cannot describe a past state — ✗ I would live in Boston. (бывало, обычно)
examples: Every summer we would drive up to the lake.
My grandfather would read the paper cover to cover.
She would never admit she was tired.

senses.head: The past of will in reported speech
body: Backshift: will inside a past-tense report becomes would. (что будет — в косвенной речи)
examples: He said he would be late.
They promised the parts would ship on Monday.
I knew she would say that.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /wəd/, contracted 'd /d/ in I'd go · the l is silent
entries.register: everyday — and the single most important modal for sounding polite
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: would — no -s, ✗ he woulds · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: Would is the past of will only in reported speech; everywhere else it is present-tense politeness or hypothesis, so a would in front of you is usually not about the past. It is a homophone of wood. Russian's бы covers most of it, but not the past-habit sense, where Russian uses бывало — and English then also allows used to. Never ✗ if I would have time: the if-clause takes the past, if I had time, I would call.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it (would go), no -s, no -ing, no participle. For a past hypothetical it stacks with have: would have gone.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — it takes a bare-infinitive complement, not an object.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: it would be finished by Friday.

entries.meaning: Nearly gone from American speech except in one construction — but that construction has no substitute.
examples: Shall I open a window?
Shall we start without him?
What shall I tell them?
The tenant shall give thirty days' notice.
Each party shall bear its own costs.
Applications shall be submitted in writing.
We shall see.
I shall never forget it.
They said they should be glad to help.

senses.head: Offers and suggestions — Shall I…? / Shall we…?
body: The living use. It asks the listener to decide whether the speaker should act. (давай…?; мне …?)
examples: Shall I open a window?
Shall we start without him?
What shall I tell them?

senses.head: Obligation in legal and formal writing
body: "Is required to." Common in contracts, statutes and specifications. (обязан, должен)
examples: The tenant shall give thirty days' notice.
Each party shall bear its own costs.
Applications shall be submitted in writing.

senses.head: Dated first-person future
body: Old-fashioned in America, still current in British English and in set phrases. (буду, будем)
examples: We shall see.
I shall never forget it.
They said they should be glad to help.

entries.register: formal or fixed — in American English it survives mainly in Shall I…? and in legal writing
entries.pattern: a — ou (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: shall — no -s, ✗ he shalls · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: The old textbook rule that shall marks the first-person future (I shall go) is dead in American speech — use will. What survives is the question Shall I…? / Shall we…?, offering to do something, where will would be wrong: ✗ Will I open the window? asks a prediction, not an offer. In contracts shall means "is required to", which is why drafters now often replace it with must.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it, no -s, no -ing, no participle.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only.
entries.passive: no — the supported verb carries voice: the fee shall be paid in advance.

entries.meaning: Advice, expectation, and — in should have — one of the few grammatical ways English has of expressing regret.
examples: You should get that looked at.
We should have left earlier.
He should apologize, and he knows it.
The train should be here any minute.
That should be enough flour for two loaves.
She should have landed by now.
I should have listened to you.
They should never have signed it.
You shouldn't have gone alone.
He asked whether he should wait.
Should you need anything, the front desk is open all night.
She wondered what she should say.

senses.head: Advice and recommendation
body: The core sense. Weaker than must, stronger than could. (следует, стоит)
examples: You should get that looked at.
We should have left earlier.
He should apologize, and he knows it.

senses.head: Expectation and probability
body: Not duty — a reasonable guess about how things will turn out. (должно быть, должен по идее)
examples: The train should be here any minute.
That should be enough flour for two loaves.
She should have landed by now.

senses.head: Regret and reproach — should have
body: Something that did not happen and ought to have. Always with the participle, never ✗ should had. (надо было бы)
examples: I should have listened to you.
They should never have signed it.
You shouldn't have gone alone.

senses.head: The past of shall in reported speech
body: Backshift, and in formal conditionals. (— в косвенной речи)
examples: He asked whether he should wait.
Should you need anything, the front desk is open all night.
She wondered what she should say.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /ʃəd/ · the l is silent
entries.register: everyday — the ordinary way to give advice
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: should — no -s, ✗ he shoulds · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: Should is advice; must and have to are obligation. Russian должен covers both, so learners overuse must and sound commanding — you should see a doctor is advice, you must see a doctor is an order. For the past, should does not become anything: use should have + participle, which always carries regret or reproach (I should have called). Spoken should've /ˈʃʊdəv/ is heard as "should of" — but never written that way.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it, no -s, no -ing, no participle. Stacks with have for the past: should have gone.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: the form should be signed.

entries.meaning: Obligation and deduction in one form — and the negative means something entirely different from the negative of have to.
examples: All passengers must show a boarding pass.
I must remember to water the plants.
You must be eighteen or older to apply.
She must be exhausted after that flight.
There's no car in the drive — they must have left.
You must be joking.
You mustn't say a word about this.
Visitors must not feed the animals.
We mustn't be late again.

senses.head: Obligation and necessity
body: A requirement, usually from a rule or from the speaker. Stronger and more impersonal than should. (должен, обязан)
examples: All passengers must show a boarding pass.
I must remember to water the plants.
You must be eighteen or older to apply.

senses.head: Logical deduction
body: Not duty at all — the speaker's certainty, reasoned from evidence. The opposite is can't, not mustn't. (должно быть)
examples: She must be exhausted after that flight.
There's no car in the drive — they must have left.
You must be joking.

senses.head: Prohibition — mustn't
body: Forbidden. Note that this is not the negative of sense 1's must in Russian terms. (нельзя)
examples: You mustn't say a word about this.
Visitors must not feed the animals.
We mustn't be late again.

entries.register: everyday — though have to has largely taken over the obligation sense in American speech
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: must — no -s, ✗ he musts · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: The trap is the negative. Mustn't is a prohibition — you mustn't tell anyone — while don't have to is the absence of obligation: you don't have to tell anyone. They are opposites, and Russian не должен sits between them. Must also has no past: for past obligation use had to (I had to leave early), and reserve must have for deduction about the past (he must have left early).
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it, no -s, no -ing, no participle, no infinitive (✗ to must). Have to supplies every missing form.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only. The noun a must ("something essential") is a separate word.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: the door must be locked.

entries.meaning: The hedge: possible but not asserted — and the reason English speakers sound noncommittal to Russian ears.
examples: It might rain later.
She might already know.
I might not make it to dinner.
He might have taken the earlier train.
We might have met before — you look familiar.
It might have been worse.
You might try turning it off and on again.
You might have told me.
I thought we might walk instead.
She said she might be late.
He asked whether he might leave early.
They warned us the road might be closed.

senses.head: Possibility
body: Something may or may not be or become true. The workhorse sense. (может быть, возможно)
examples: It might rain later.
She might already know.
I might not make it to dinner.

senses.head: Past possibility — might have
body: A guess about something already settled. (мог бы; возможно, …)
examples: He might have taken the earlier train.
We might have met before — you look familiar.
It might have been worse.

senses.head: Tentative suggestions and reproach
body: Softening a proposal, or — with stress — complaining that something was not done. (мог бы)
examples: You might try turning it off and on again.
You might have told me.
I thought we might walk instead.

senses.head: The past of may in reported speech
body: Backshift. (— в косвенной речи)
examples: She said she might be late.
He asked whether he might leave early.
They warned us the road might be closed.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary way to hedge
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: might — no -s, ✗ he mights · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: Might and may are near-identical in American English for possibility; might is slightly more tentative and far commoner in speech. It is not usually past — he might come is about now. For the past, might have + participle (he might have missed the train). It is a homograph of the noun might ("strength"), as in with all his might.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it, no -s, no -ing, no participle. Stacks with have for the past: might have gone.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: it might be canceled.

entries.meaning: The politeness modal — and the one whose past-tense form misleads learners most, because three of its four senses are about the present.
examples: Could you hold this for a second?
Could I ask you something?
Could we move the meeting to Thursday?
We could take the coast road instead.
That could be the mail carrier.
You could always ask her yourself.
She could read before she started school.
We couldn't see the stage from where we sat.
He could run a mile in under six minutes back then.
You could have been hurt.
I could have sworn I locked it.
They couldn't have known.

senses.head: Polite requests
body: Present time. The most frequent use of the word, and the safest register for a stranger. (не могли бы вы)
examples: Could you hold this for a second?
Could I ask you something?
Could we move the meeting to Thursday?

senses.head: Possibility and suggestion
body: Weaker than will, close to might, and the ordinary way to float an idea. (мог бы, можно бы)
examples: We could take the coast road instead.
That could be the mail carrier.
You could always ask her yourself.

senses.head: Past ability
body: A general capacity in the past, not a one-time success. (мог, умел)
examples: She could read before she started school.
We couldn't see the stage from where we sat.
He could run a mile in under six minutes back then.

senses.head: Unreal past — could have
body: Something possible that did not happen, often with reproach or relief. (мог бы)
examples: You could have been hurt.
I could have sworn I locked it.
They couldn't have known.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /kəd/ · the l is silent
entries.русский: мог бы, мог; не могли бы вы
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: could — no -s, ✗ he coulds · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: Could is the past of can only for general past ability (I could swim at four). For a single past success English switches to was able to or managed to: ✗ I could catch the train yesterday → I managed to catch it. And most coulds are not past at all — Could you help me? is a present request. There is no participle: ✗ I have could.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — bare infinitive after it, no -s, no -ing, no participle. Stacks with have: could have gone.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: it could be repaired.

entries.meaning: The only modal that keeps to — and a near-twin of should that survives mostly in speech.
examples: You ought to tell her the truth.
We ought to leave a tip.
Somebody ought to fix that step.
That ought to be enough for four people.
The paint ought to be dry by morning.
This ought to only take a minute.
I ought to have said something.
They ought to have warned us.
You oughtn't to have gone alone.

senses.head: Duty and advice
body: What is right or sensible to do. (следует, надо бы)
examples: You ought to tell her the truth.
We ought to leave a tip.
Somebody ought to fix that step.

senses.head: Expectation
body: A reasonable prediction, exactly like should. (должно быть, по идее)
examples: That ought to be enough for four people.
The paint ought to be dry by morning.
This ought to only take a minute.

senses.head: Unfulfilled duty — ought to have
body: Regret, identical in force to should have. (надо было бы)
examples: I ought to have said something.
They ought to have warned us.
You oughtn't to have gone alone.

entries.forms: ought to /ˈɔːt tə/ · — · — (no past, no participle)
entries.register: everyday but slightly old-fashioned — should has largely replaced it
entries.pattern: defective (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: ought to — no -s, ✗ he oughts · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: The one modal that keeps its to — ought to go, where every other modal takes a bare infinitive. Meaning is all but identical to should, and should is commoner in American English; ought to leans a little more toward moral duty. The negative oughtn't and the question Ought I…? both sound stiff — Americans switch to shouldn't and Should I…?
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — but with a to-infinitive, not a bare one. No -s, no -ing, no participle. Stacks with have: ought to have gone.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — infinitival complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: it ought to be reported.

entries.meaning: Past habit and past state, both marked as over — the construction that says "and not anymore" without saying it.
examples: We used to eat dinner at six sharp.
She used to walk to work before the office moved.
I used to smoke, but I quit years ago.
There used to be a bakery on this corner.
He used to be much heavier.
This used to be farmland.
Did you use to play an instrument?
It didn't use to cost this much.
Didn't she use to work here?

senses.head: Discontinued habit
body: Something done repeatedly then, not now. (раньше, бывало)
examples: We used to eat dinner at six sharp.
She used to walk to work before the office moved.
I used to smoke, but I quit years ago.

senses.head: Discontinued state
body: A condition that has since changed — where would cannot be substituted. (раньше был, когда-то)
examples: There used to be a bakery on this corner.
He used to be much heavier.
This used to be farmland.

senses.head: Questions and negatives — use to
body: The -d is carried by did, so the main form loses it. (раньше …? раньше не …)
examples: Did you use to play an instrument?
It didn't use to cost this much.
Didn't she use to work here?

entries.pronunciation note: note the /s/, not /z/ — unlike the verb used /juːzd/
entries.русский: раньше, бывало (о прошлой привычке или состоянии)
entries.forms: used to /ˈjuːst tə/ · — · — (past only; there is no present use to)
entries.register: everyday — the standard way to mark a discontinued past
entries.third person: used to — no change, ✗ he uses to · -ing form: none
entries.contrast: Two different words are spelled used. The semi-modal here is /juːst/ with an s and means "formerly"; the ordinary verb use /juːz/ → used /juːzd/ means "employ". A third, be used to /juːst/ + -ing, means "be accustomed to" — I'm used to waking early is not the same as I used to wake early. In questions and negatives the -d disappears: Did you use to live here?, I didn't use to like it. Unlike would, used to works with states: I used to have long hair is fine, ✗ I would have long hair is not.
entries.verb type: semi-modal — takes a to-infinitive and exists only in the past. Would covers the repeated-action half of its meaning but not the state half.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — infinitival complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: the building used to be a school.

entries.meaning: Advice with a threat behind it — the had is not past, and the negative goes in a place learners never guess.
examples: You 'd better leave now if you want a seat.
We 'd better check the gate number again.
He 'd better have a good explanation.
You 'd better not be late.
They 'd better not find out from someone else.
I 'd better not say anything.

senses.head: Urgent advice or warning
body: Present or future. The implied clause is "or something bad happens". (лучше бы)
examples: You 'd better leave now if you want a seat.
We 'd better check the gate number again.
He 'd better have a good explanation.

senses.head: The negative — had better not
body: Not follows better, never had. (лучше не)
examples: You 'd better not be late.
They 'd better not find out from someone else.
I 'd better not say anything.

entries.pronunciation note: usually contracted to 'd better /d ˈbɛtər/, and in fast speech to better
entries.русский: лучше бы, следовало бы (с оттенком предупреждения)
entries.forms: had better /hæd ˈbɛtər/ · — · — (one form only, despite the had)
entries.register: everyday — but carries a warning, so not neutral advice
entries.third person: had better — no change, ✗ he has better · -ing form: none
entries.contrast: The had is frozen — it is not a past tense, and had better refers to the present or future: you'd better hurry means now. It takes a bare infinitive, never to: ✗ you'd better to go. The negative puts not after better: you'd better not say anything, not ✗ you hadn't better. And it is stronger than should — it implies a bad consequence if ignored, which makes it a poor choice for gentle advice.
entries.verb type: semi-modal — bare infinitive after it, no inflection at all.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive complement only.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: this had better be fixed by Monday.

entries.meaning: Preference — and the construction where English suddenly demands a past tense for a present wish.
examples: I 'd rather stay in tonight.
She 'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
Would you rather sit inside or out?
I 'd rather you didn't mention it.
She 'd rather we came on Sunday.
They 'd rather nobody knew yet.
I 'd rather have heard it from you.
He 'd rather you hadn't told her.
We 'd rather have paid more and gotten it right.

senses.head: Simple preference
body: Same subject, bare infinitive, than for the comparison. (предпочёл бы)
examples: I 'd rather stay in tonight.
She 'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
Would you rather sit inside or out?

senses.head: Preference about someone else
body: Different subject, and the verb goes into the past although the meaning is present. (я бы предпочёл, чтобы…)
examples: I 'd rather you didn't mention it.
She 'd rather we came on Sunday.
They 'd rather nobody knew yet.

senses.head: Preference about the past
body: Would rather have + participle, or a past-perfect clause. (лучше бы)
examples: I 'd rather have heard it from you.
He 'd rather you hadn't told her.
We 'd rather have paid more and gotten it right.

entries.register: everyday — the standard way to state a preference politely
entries.third person: would rather — no change, ✗ he woulds rather · -ing form: none
entries.contrast: Bare infinitive, never to: ✗ I'd rather to stay. Comparison uses than, not that: I'd rather walk than drive. The real trap is the two-subject form — when the preference is about someone else, English switches to a past-tense clause: I'd rather you didn't (not ✗ I'd rather you don't), and for the past, I'd rather you hadn't. Would prefer is the close synonym but takes to: I'd prefer to walk.
entries.verb type: semi-modal — bare infinitive when the subject is the same, a past-tense clause when it differs.
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive — bare-infinitive or clausal complement.
entries.passive: no — voice sits on the supported verb: I'd rather be told directly.
